title: Sepsis and Septic Shock: Recognize Deterioration Early
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection. New hypotension, altered mentation, tachypnea, hypoxemia, oliguria, mottling, or poor perfusion in a patient with possible infection requires immediate escalation and treatment; no single biomarker or screening score rules sepsis in or out.
recognize: Older or immunocompromised patients may deteriorate without high fever.
Capillary refill, mental status, urine output, blood pressure, respiratory status, and lactate can help assess perfusion in context.
Septic shock is sepsis with persistent circulatory/metabolic dysfunction requiring vasopressor-level support despite initial resuscitation.
priorities: Activate the sepsis/rapid-response pathway and assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, perfusion, and likely infection source.
Obtain ordered blood cultures as soon as possible and ideally before antibiotics when this does not cause harmful delay.
Administer ordered antimicrobials and IV crystalloid promptly and reassess frequently for both under- and over-resuscitation.
assessMonitor: Trend BP/MAP, capillary refill, mental status, respiratory rate, oxygenation, urine output, lactate when ordered, temperature, skin perfusion, and response to fluids/vasopressors.
interventions: Prepare for source-control procedures when an anatomic source requires drainage, removal, or surgery.
If shock persists, anticipate vasopressor support; current adult sepsis guidance recommends norepinephrine as first-line vasopressor.
medicationSafety: Antibiotic selection should match likely source, severity, local resistance, allergies, and organ function; de-escalation follows culture/clinical data.
Fluid resuscitation is not a one-time automatic volume; reassess repeatedly for pulmonary edema and perfusion response.
teaching: After recovery, teach that weakness, cognitive changes, sleep problems, mood symptoms, and functional decline can persist and deserve follow-up.
delegationScope: Routine vital-sign collection may be delegated with explicit thresholds, but suspected sepsis and any deterioration require immediate licensed-nurse assessment and escalation.
examTrap: Waiting for a positive culture or fever before escalating a patient with infection plus new organ dysfunction.
oneLinePearl: Infection + new organ dysfunction = treat sepsis as an emergency.
sourceBasis: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026

title: Hypovolemic Shock: Restore Circulating Volume
bottomLine: Hypovolemic shock results from inadequate circulating volume due to blood or fluid loss. Tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure, cool clammy skin, delayed capillary refill, oliguria, altered mentation, and eventually hypotension require rapid control of the cause and restoration of perfusion.
recognize: Hemorrhage may be external or hidden in the chest, abdomen, pelvis, retroperitoneum, GI tract, or tissues.
Children and younger adults can maintain blood pressure until substantial volume has been lost.
priorities: Assess ABCs and identify/stop ongoing losses when possible.
Establish/maintain ordered large-bore vascular access and begin prescribed fluid or blood resuscitation.
Keep the patient warm and prepare for definitive hemorrhage or source control.
assessMonitor: Trend mental status, heart rate, BP, pulse pressure, capillary refill, skin temperature, urine output, bleeding, and response to resuscitation.
interventions: Apply direct pressure to compressible external hemorrhage and use approved hemorrhage-control measures when indicated.
Do not delay definitive bleeding control because transient BP improvement occurs after fluids.
medicationSafety: Blood products require transfusion-safety procedures and monitoring.
Excess crystalloid can dilute clotting factors and worsen edema in major hemorrhage; follow the trauma/hemorrhage protocol.
teaching: After stabilization, reinforce medication and follow-up plans related to the cause of bleeding or fluid loss.
delegationScope: Shock is unstable care and requires licensed-nurse assessment; delegated tasks must not delay resuscitation or reassessment.
examTrap: Assuming a normal blood pressure excludes significant shock in a patient who is tachycardic, cool, confused, and oliguric.
oneLinePearl: Perfusion falls before pressure always does.
sourceBasis: American College of Surgeons trauma resuscitation principles

title: Cardiogenic Shock: Pump Failure
bottomLine: Cardiogenic shock is severe pump failure causing inadequate organ perfusion, often after acute MI or major cardiac dysfunction. Hypotension plus cool clammy skin, oliguria, altered mentation, pulmonary congestion, chest pain, or dysrhythmia requires emergency escalation; indiscriminate large fluid boluses can worsen pulmonary edema.
recognize: Crackles, elevated JVP, pulmonary edema, cool extremities, weak pulses, and altered mentation point toward low cardiac output with congestion.
Mechanical complications after MI can cause sudden shock and new murmurs.
priorities: Activate emergency/cardiac response and assess airway, breathing, circulation, ECG/rhythm, perfusion, and chest pain.
Provide oxygen for hypoxemia and prepare for urgent reperfusion or mechanical-cause evaluation.
Administer fluids, vasopressors, inotropes, and diuretics only according to the hemodynamic plan.
assessMonitor: Continuous ECG/hemodynamic monitoring, urine output, mental status, oxygenation, lung sounds, perfusion, and response to therapy.
interventions: Maintain rest and minimize myocardial oxygen demand while definitive treatment is arranged.
Prepare for advanced circulatory support when ordered.
medicationSafety: Nitrates and aggressive diuresis can worsen hypotension in shock.
Large empiric fluid boluses may worsen pulmonary edema when pump failure is the problem.
teaching: After stabilization, reinforce heart-failure/ACS secondary-prevention plans and rapid reporting of recurrent chest pain or dyspnea.
delegationScope: Cardiogenic shock is unstable and requires continuous licensed-nurse assessment and immediate RN/provider/cardiology collaboration.
examTrap: Treating every shock state with a large fluid bolus without considering pulmonary congestion and pump failure.
oneLinePearl: Shock + wet lungs = think failing pump before pouring in fluid.
sourceBasis: ACC/AHA acute myocardial infarction and cardiogenic shock guidance

title: Hyperkalemia: Protect the Heart
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Hyperkalemia can cause fatal dysrhythmias. Significant elevation, weakness, bradycardia, conduction changes, peaked T waves, widening QRS, or renal failure requires urgent cardiac monitoring and treatment; a hemolyzed specimen should be repeated when the clinical picture does not fit, but dangerous ECG changes are not ignored while waiting.
recognize: Risk rises with kidney failure, potassium supplements, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, tissue breakdown, and acidosis.
ECG changes are neither perfectly sensitive nor specific, so severity is judged using the whole clinical context.
priorities: Stop exogenous potassium sources when ordered and notify the RN/provider for significant elevation or ECG change.
Place on cardiac monitoring when severe or symptomatic.
Prepare for ordered therapies that stabilize myocardium, shift potassium intracellularly, and remove potassium from the body.
assessMonitor: Trend potassium, glucose during insulin therapy, ECG/rhythm, renal function, urine output, acid-base status, and recurrence after temporizing treatment.
interventions: IV calcium may be ordered to stabilize the myocardium when dangerous ECG changes are present; it does not remove potassium.
Insulin with glucose shifts potassium into cells and requires glucose surveillance; definitive removal may require diuresis, binders, or dialysis depending on the patient.
medicationSafety: Verify that IV potassium is not being administered during hyperkalemia.
Insulin treatment can cause hypoglycemia; glucose monitoring is essential.
teaching: Patients with kidney disease should follow individualized potassium and medication guidance rather than avoiding all potassium-containing foods indiscriminately.
delegationScope: Routine lab collection can be delegated, but critical potassium values and ECG changes require immediate licensed-nurse assessment and escalation.
examTrap: Thinking calcium lowers the serum potassium; its urgent role is myocardial stabilization.
oneLinePearl: Hyperkalemia kills electrically—monitor the heart while fixing the potassium.
sourceBasis: 2025 American Heart Association Special Circumstances of Resuscitation

title: Hypokalemia: Muscles and Rhythm
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Low potassium can impair skeletal, GI, and cardiac muscle function and increase dysrhythmia risk. Identify losses or medication causes, replace potassium safely, monitor magnesium and rhythm when indicated, and never give IV potassium by direct IV push.
recognize: Diuretics, vomiting/diarrhea, poor intake, alkalosis, insulin shifts, and magnesium deficiency can contribute.
Weakness, cramps, ileus/constipation, palpitations, and ECG changes may occur.
priorities: Assess rhythm, weakness, GI function, losses, medications, and renal function.
Replace potassium according to the ordered route/rate and recheck levels.
Evaluate magnesium when hypokalemia is persistent or difficult to correct.
assessMonitor: Trend potassium, magnesium, ECG when significantly low, renal function, urine output, GI losses, and response to replacement.
interventions: Use oral replacement when appropriate and tolerated; IV replacement requires dilution, pump control, and rate limits per facility policy.
Correct ongoing causes such as diarrhea or medication-related losses when possible.
medicationSafety: Never administer concentrated potassium as an IV push.
Digoxin-associated dysrhythmia risk increases when potassium is low.
teaching: Follow individualized food and supplement advice; patients with kidney disease should not self-increase potassium without guidance.
delegationScope: IV potassium administration scope varies by state/facility for LPN/LVN practice; abnormal results and symptoms require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Giving IV potassium rapidly because the laboratory value is very low.
oneLinePearl: Low K slows muscles and destabilizes rhythm—replace safely, never IV push.

title: Hyponatremia: Brain Symptoms Matter
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Hyponatremia is usually a water-balance problem rather than simply too little dietary salt. Headache, vomiting, confusion, seizures, or reduced consciousness suggest cerebral edema and require urgent management; correction must be controlled because overly rapid sodium rise can cause severe neurologic injury.
recognize: Causes include excess free water, SIADH, heart/liver/kidney disease, diuretics, GI losses with replacement by water, and endocrine disorders.
Symptom severity depends on both sodium level and how rapidly it fell.
priorities: Assess neurologic status, volume status, medications, fluid intake/losses, and seizure risk.
Institute seizure precautions for severe symptomatic cases and escalate immediately.
Follow the ordered fluid strategy and sodium-correction plan; do not improvise with salt or water restriction.
assessMonitor: Trend sodium at the ordered frequency, neurologic status, intake/output, daily weight, urine studies when ordered, and volume status.
interventions: Fluid restriction may be used for selected dilutional causes; isotonic or hypertonic saline is used only for specific indications and with close monitoring.
medicationSafety: Thiazide diuretics and some psychotropic medications can contribute.
Rapid overcorrection can cause osmotic demyelination, especially in high-risk chronic hyponatremia.
redFlags: Very low sodium with neurologic symptoms
teaching: Do not self-treat chronic low sodium by adding large amounts of salt or sharply restricting water without a clinician-directed plan.
delegationScope: Fluid-intake measurements may be delegated, but neurologic changes and sodium correction require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Assuming hyponatremia always means the patient needs salty food.
oneLinePearl: Low sodium is often too much water—and the brain tells you when it is dangerous.

title: Hypocalcemia: Neuromuscular Irritability
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Low ionized calcium increases neuromuscular excitability. Perioral/finger tingling, cramps, tetany, carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm, seizures, or QT prolongation require assessment of calcium, magnesium, renal/parathyroid status, and urgent replacement when severe or symptomatic.
recognize: Risk can follow thyroid/parathyroid surgery, severe vitamin D deficiency, kidney disease, pancreatitis, massive transfusion, or hypomagnesemia.
Total calcium can be misleading when albumin is abnormal; ionized calcium may better reflect biologically active calcium.
priorities: Assess airway, neuromuscular symptoms, seizure activity, and rhythm in severe cases.
Escalate stridor/laryngospasm, seizure, or significant ECG change immediately.
Administer calcium replacement according to severity and route ordered.
assessMonitor: Trend calcium/ionized calcium, magnesium, phosphate, ECG when severe, and symptoms after replacement.
interventions: Use seizure/fall precautions when neuromuscular irritability is significant.
Correct associated magnesium deficiency when ordered because it can make hypocalcemia refractory.
medicationSafety: IV calcium can cause tissue injury with extravasation and requires controlled administration/monitoring.
Calcium products and compatibility require attention in IV therapy.
teaching: After parathyroid/thyroid surgery, report tingling around the mouth or fingers, spasms, or breathing difficulty promptly.
delegationScope: New neuromuscular or airway symptoms require licensed-nurse assessment; IV calcium scope varies by state/facility.
examTrap: Treating stridor after thyroid surgery as routine postoperative throat irritation.
oneLinePearl: Tingling to tetany to airway—hypocalcemia can escalate quickly.
sourceBasis: National Institutes of Health calcium physiology resources

title: Heat Stroke: Cool Now
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Heat stroke is hyperthermia with central nervous system dysfunction and is a medical emergency. Confusion, ataxia, seizures, collapse, or altered consciousness after heat exposure requires immediate emergency activation and rapid cooling; do not delay cooling while waiting for transport or a perfect core-temperature measurement.
recognize: Skin may be hot and dry or sweaty; absence of sweating is not required.
Exertional heat stroke may affect young healthy people, while classic heat stroke often affects older adults or people with chronic disease/medication risk.
priorities: Call EMS/activate emergency response and move the patient out of the heat.
Begin rapid active cooling immediately using the best available method.
Assess airway, breathing, circulation, glucose, mental status, and complications.
assessMonitor: Core temperature when available, neurologic status, hemodynamics, glucose, renal/liver function, electrolytes, coagulation, and urine output in acute care.
interventions: Cold-water immersion is highly effective for exertional heat stroke when feasible; other aggressive evaporative/conductive cooling methods are used based on setting and patient factors.
Avoid shivering-promoting or ineffective delay-prone cooling approaches.
medicationSafety: Antipyretics such as acetaminophen do not treat heat stroke because the problem is not a raised hypothalamic set point.
teaching: Heat acclimatization, hydration plans, rest breaks, cooling access, and medication-risk review reduce preventable heat illness.
delegationScope: Anyone can initiate emergency cooling and call for help; ongoing unstable assessment requires licensed-nurse/EMS management.
examTrap: Giving acetaminophen and waiting instead of initiating rapid physical cooling.
oneLinePearl: Heat stroke = hot brain: cool first and fast.
sourceBasis: 2025 American Heart Association Special Circumstances of Resuscitation

title: Hypothermia: Handle Gently and Rewarm
bottomLine: Moderate or severe hypothermia can cause bradycardia, dysrhythmias, altered consciousness, respiratory depression, and cardiac arrest. Remove wet clothing, prevent further heat loss, handle gently, use appropriate active rewarming, and follow hypothermia-specific resuscitation protocols.
recognize: Shivering may diminish as hypothermia becomes severe.
A profoundly cold patient can have very slow pulse and respirations, requiring careful assessment rather than assuming death.
priorities: Assess airway, breathing, circulation carefully and activate emergency care for moderate/severe hypothermia.
Remove wet garments, insulate, and rewarm the trunk/core preferentially.
Handle gently because severe hypothermia increases dysrhythmia risk.
assessMonitor: Core temperature when available, rhythm, glucose, oxygenation, mental status, perfusion, and rewarming response.
interventions: Use passive external rewarming for mild cases and active external/internal rewarming for more severe cases according to setting and protocol.
Treat associated hypoglycemia, trauma, intoxication, or exposure complications.
medicationSafety: Resuscitation medication timing and defibrillation strategies can differ in severe hypothermia; follow current advanced-resuscitation guidance.
redFlags: Absent shivering with marked cold exposure
teaching: Layer clothing, stay dry, avoid alcohol as a warming strategy, and seek care for confusion or severe exposure symptoms.
delegationScope: Emergency warming measures may be initiated by trained staff, but severe hypothermia requires continuous licensed/EMS assessment.
examTrap: Rubbing or rapidly heating cold extremities while neglecting core rewarming and gentle handling.
oneLinePearl: Cold heart, gentle hands, warm the core.
sourceBasis: 2025 American Heart Association Special Circumstances of Resuscitation

title: Rhabdomyolysis: Muscle Breakdown Threatens Kidneys
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Rhabdomyolysis releases muscle contents that can cause hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury. Severe muscle pain/weakness, swelling, or dark urine after crush injury, prolonged immobilization, extreme exertion, heat illness, seizure, ischemia, or certain drugs requires urgent CK, renal, potassium, and fluid-status evaluation.
recognize: The classic triad of muscle pain, weakness, and dark urine is not always present.
Potassium can rise rapidly and become the immediate life threat.
priorities: Assess cause, perfusion, urine output, rhythm, potassium, renal function, and compartment-syndrome signs.
Administer ordered IV fluids and monitor response.
Escalate significant hyperkalemia, oliguria, or compartment syndrome promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend CK, creatinine, potassium, calcium/phosphate, urine output/color, ECG when indicated, and volume status.
interventions: Treat the precipitating cause and avoid additional nephrotoxins when possible.
Balance aggressive hydration with heart/kidney function and risk of fluid overload.
medicationSafety: Medication-associated rhabdomyolysis requires clinician review; do not independently discontinue essential therapy unless emergency protocol directs it.
redFlags: Severe limb swelling with pain on passive stretch
teaching: Seek care for severe muscle symptoms or dark urine after extreme exertion/heat illness or when taking a medication associated with muscle injury.
delegationScope: Urine measurement may be delegated, but critical electrolyte/renal changes require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Focusing on dark urine while missing hyperkalemia and compartment syndrome.
oneLinePearl: Broken muscle spills potassium and myoglobin—protect heart and kidneys.
sourceBasis: National Kidney Foundation acute kidney injury resources
